unitPlan.title: Lumière et chaleur hivernales
unitPlan.bigIdeas: Explorer les sources d'énergie et comprendre comment la lumière et la chaleur affectent notre vie quotidienne en hiver

lessons.title: Lumière tout autour de nous
lessons.oneGoal: Students will identify different sources of light in their environment and understand that light is needed to see things

decisionPoints.question: What light sources are most visible and safe for students to observe in the classroom?
decisionPoints.guidance: If bright classroom: Focus on comparing light sources. If dim classroom: Add more artificial lights for better observation.

decisionPoints.question: Should we start with natural light sources or artificial ones?
decisionPoints.guidance: If sunny day: Begin with sunlight through windows. If cloudy/dark: Start with classroom lights and flashlights.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for simple light/dark comparisons?
decisionPoints.guidance: If understanding well: Add light intensity comparisons. If struggling: Focus on light present vs absent only.

lessons.opening: Light detective game (5 min): Turn off all classroom lights. Ask 'Qu'est-ce qui se passe? Pourquoi ne pouvons-nous pas bien voir?' Turn lights back on. Introduce: 'Nous avons besoin de lumière pour voir!'
lessons.mainActivity: Light source hunt (25 min): Students explore classroom and nearby areas to find light sources. Use clipboards to draw or check off: sun through windows, overhead lights, computer screens, flashlights. Create class chart categorizing light sources. Practice vocabulary: 'Cette lumière vient du...' Students test vision by looking at books in bright vs dim areas. Compare what happens when they cover/uncover light sources.
lessons.closing: Light celebration circle (10 min): Students share their favorite light source and explain why we need it. Sing simple song about light helping us see: 'La lumière, la lumière, nous aide à tout voir!'
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If students get scared in darkness: Keep activity very brief. If too many light sources: Focus on 3-4 main categories. If vision testing difficult: Use obvious contrasts like white paper vs black paper.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students recognize how they use different lights at home: lamps for reading, kitchen lights for cooking, flashlights when power goes out
lessons.visualSupports: Light source picture cards, light/dark comparison photos, hand gestures for 'bright' (hands spread wide) and 'dark' (hands over eyes)

lessons.title: Le soleil - notre grande source de lumière
lessons.oneGoal: Students will understand that the sun is our most important source of light and provides heat

decisionPoints.question: How can we safely observe sunlight without looking directly at the sun?
decisionPoints.guidance: If sunny day: Use shadows and indirect observation. If cloudy: Use photos and videos of sunny conditions.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on light or heat properties of the sun first?
decisionPoints.guidance: If temperature differences obvious: Start with heat. If light more noticeable: Begin with brightness and visibility.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready to understand the sun as both light and heat source?
decisionPoints.guidance: If concepts connecting well: Explore both properties together. If overwhelming: Focus on one property per activity.

lessons.opening: Sun safety demonstration (5 min): Show how we never look directly at the sun (use props, not real sun). Demonstrate safe ways to observe sunlight: shadows, feeling warmth, seeing brightness on surfaces.
lessons.mainActivity: Solar exploration (25 min): Students safely explore sun's effects: feel warmth of sunlight on hands vs shade, observe how sunlight makes objects visible vs shadowy areas, compare temperature of objects in sun vs shade. Use thermometers or hand tests to compare warm sunny spots to cool shady areas. Create sun observation journal with drawings of sun's light and heat effects. Practice saying: 'Le soleil nous donne la lumière et la chaleur.'
lessons.closing: Sun appreciation ceremony (10 min): Students share how the sun helps them (provides light to see, warmth to feel comfortable). Create movements for sun's light (arms spreading wide) and heat (hands warming together).
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If no direct sunlight available: Use heat lamps or warm/cool comparisons. If thermometers too complex: Focus on feeling temperature differences. If sun concepts abstract: Use lots of concrete examples and props.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand why sunny days feel warmer and brighter, and why we need the sun for daylight
lessons.visualSupports: Sun safety picture cards, temperature comparison charts showing sunny vs shady areas, sun effects diagram

lessons.title: Ombres magiques
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe how shadows form when objects block light and experiment with making different shadows

decisionPoints.question: What objects create the clearest, most interesting shadows for young learners?
decisionPoints.guidance: If clear shadows needed: Use solid, simple shapes. If creativity wanted: Provide varied objects including transparent and translucent items.

decisionPoints.question: Should we use flashlights or natural sunlight for shadow experiments?
decisionPoints.guidance: If sunlight available: Use natural shadows for authenticity. If indoor/cloudy: Flashlights provide controlled shadow-making.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for shadow size and direction observations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If observation skills strong: Include size and direction changes. If basic understanding needed: Focus on presence/absence of shadows.

lessons.opening: Shadow puppet introduction (5 min): Teacher creates simple shadow puppet on wall using flashlight and hands. Ask students to guess what makes the shadow appear and disappear.
lessons.mainActivity: Shadow laboratory (25 min): Set up shadow stations with flashlights and various objects (toys, shapes, hands). Students experiment making shadows on wall or paper. Observe what happens when they move objects closer/farther from light source. Try making shadows with transparent vs opaque objects. Practice vocabulary: 'L'objet bloque la lumière', 'Voici mon ombre'. Create shadow art by tracing around shadows of interesting objects.
lessons.closing: Shadow story circle (10 min): Students use their hands to create shadow animals and tell mini-stories. Discuss how shadows show that light travels in straight lines and can be blocked.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If shadows unclear: Ensure strong light source and dark background. If students get distracted: Use timer for station rotations. If objects create confusion: Start with very simple shapes only.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students notice their own shadows when walking outside and understand shadow play games
lessons.visualSupports: Shadow formation diagram showing light-object-shadow relationship, shadow size comparison pictures, step-by-step shadow making instructions

lessons.title: Expérience avec les ombres
lessons.oneGoal: Students will conduct experiments to discover how shadow size changes when objects move closer or farther from light sources

decisionPoints.question: What safe objects work best for distance-shadow experiments?
decisionPoints.guidance: If fine motor skills developing: Use larger objects that are easy to hold. If advanced: Try smaller objects for more precise observations.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on shadow size or shadow clarity changes?
decisionPoints.guidance: If size changes obvious: Emphasize big/small comparisons. If clarity more noticeable: Discuss sharp vs fuzzy shadow edges.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for making predictions about shadow changes?
decisionPoints.guidance: If prediction skills emerging: Ask simple 'What do you think will happen?' If advanced: Have students explain their reasoning.

lessons.opening: Shadow prediction circle (5 min): Show object and flashlight. Ask students to predict what will happen to shadow size if object moves closer to light, then farther away.
lessons.mainActivity: Shadow size experiment (25 min): Students work in pairs with flashlights and identical objects. Move objects to different distances from light source and observe shadow changes. Use measuring tools (blocks, paper strips) to compare shadow sizes. Record observations with drawings showing small, medium, and large shadows. Practice vocabulary: 'Plus proche = ombre plus grande', 'Plus loin = ombre plus petite'. Create shadow size comparison charts.
lessons.closing: Experiment sharing (10 min): Students demonstrate their shadow discoveries to class. Discuss findings: objects closer to light make bigger shadows, objects farther make smaller shadows.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If distance concepts confusing: Use obvious close/far positions. If measuring difficult: Focus on big/medium/small comparisons. If flashlight batteries weak: Have backup lights available.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand why their shadows look different sizes at different times of day when sun is high or low
lessons.visualSupports: Shadow size sequence pictures, distance demonstration setup diagram, prediction vs observation recording sheets

lessons.title: Lumières artificielles dans notre maison
lessons.oneGoal: Students will identify and compare different artificial light sources used in homes and understand their purposes

decisionPoints.question: Which artificial light sources are most familiar to students?
decisionPoints.guidance: If common lights known: Focus on purpose and function. If variety limited: Use pictures to expand awareness of different light types.

decisionPoints.question: Should we compare brightness levels or focus on different purposes?
decisionPoints.guidance: If brightness obvious: Include bright/dim comparisons. If purpose more relevant: Emphasize when/why different lights are used.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for energy usage discussions?
decisionPoints.guidance: If energy concepts emerging: Introduce simple on/off and power ideas. If too complex: Focus only on identification and use.

lessons.opening: Home light tour (5 min): Students close eyes and imagine walking through their house at night. What lights would they turn on in each room? Share responses.
lessons.mainActivity: Artificial light exploration (25 min): Examine various artificial lights in classroom and pictures of home lights: overhead lights, lamps, flashlights, computer screens, candles (safely). Sort lights by brightness, size, or purpose. Create home light map showing which lights are used in different rooms. Practice naming lights and their purposes: 'Cette lampe éclaire pour lire', 'Cette lumière éclaire toute la pièce'. Compare battery vs plug-in lights.
lessons.closing: Light purpose game (10 min): Teacher shows picture of activity (reading, cooking, walking in dark) and students suggest which artificial light would be most helpful.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If too many light types: Focus on 4-5 most common ones. If purpose concepts difficult: Use simple activity matching. If safety concerns: Ensure all demonstrations use safe, battery-powered lights.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students recognize and name lights they use daily: bedroom lamps, kitchen lights, bathroom lights, flashlights for camping
lessons.visualSupports: Home lighting picture cards, light purpose matching charts, room-by-room lighting diagrams

lessons.title: Quand avons-nous besoin de lumière artificielle?
lessons.oneGoal: Students will understand when artificial lights are needed and why we use them in winter and at night

decisionPoints.question: How can we demonstrate the need for artificial light in age-appropriate ways?
decisionPoints.guidance: If concepts clear: Use time and season comparisons. If abstract: Focus on obvious dark vs light situations.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on seasonal light changes or daily light cycles?
decisionPoints.guidance: If seasonal changes noticeable: Emphasize winter daylight differences. If daily cycles more obvious: Focus on day/night patterns.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for comparing winter and summer light needs?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comparison skills strong: Create detailed season contrasts. If developing: Use simple 'more lights in winter' concept.

lessons.opening: Light needs demonstration (5 min): Simulate different scenarios with room lights: bright sunny day (lights off), cloudy day (some lights), nighttime (all lights on), winter evening (extra lights).
lessons.mainActivity: Light timing investigation (25 min): Create timeline showing when artificial lights are needed throughout day and seasons. Compare summer vs winter evening activities - when do we turn on lights? Use pictures showing same activities in different lighting conditions. Students draw themselves doing evening activities with and without artificial lights. Practice vocabulary: 'En hiver, nous avons besoin de plus de lumière', 'La nuit, nous allumons les lumières'.
lessons.closing: Light schedule creation (10 min): Create class schedule showing when artificial lights are most needed during school day. Plan to observe and record light usage over one day.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If time concepts difficult: Use very obvious light/dark examples. If seasonal changes subtle: Use clear photo comparisons. If tracking complex: Focus on simple on/off observations.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand why lights are on when they get home from school in winter but not in summer
lessons.visualSupports: Daily light timeline with pictures, seasonal lighting comparison charts, light usage tracking sheets with visual cues

lessons.title: La chaleur du soleil
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe and measure how the sun provides heat and understand that heat comes from the sun's light

decisionPoints.question: What safe methods can demonstrate solar heat for Grade 1 students?
decisionPoints.guidance: If sunny conditions: Use direct sun/shade comparisons. If limited sun: Use heat lamps or warm/cool object comparisons.

decisionPoints.question: Should we use thermometers or focus on feeling temperature differences?
decisionPoints.guidance: If thermometer skills developing: Include simple temperature reading. If too complex: Focus on touch and feeling warmth.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for simple temperature measurement activities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If measurement skills emerging: Use large, simple thermometers. If advanced: Try recording temperature differences numerically.

lessons.opening: Solar warming experiment (5 min): Place one hand in sunny area and one in shade. Students describe feelings: 'chaud, tiède, froid'. Introduce that sun gives us heat as well as light.
lessons.mainActivity: Heat detection investigation (25 min): Use thermometers or touch tests to compare temperatures: objects in sun vs shade, water in sunny vs shaded containers, different surfaces (metal, plastic, wood) after sun exposure. Students predict which will be warmer and test their predictions. Create heat detection journals recording observations. Practice vocabulary: 'Le soleil réchauffe', 'Cette surface est chaude', 'La température monte'. Explore how sun's heat helps us feel warm outside.
lessons.closing: Solar heat demonstration (10 min): Students share discoveries about sun's heating power. Create movements showing how sun warms Earth (arms spreading warmth) and discuss why sunny days feel warmer than cloudy days.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If thermometers too complex: Use simple warm/cool comparisons. If limited sun: Use artificial heat sources carefully. If concepts abstract: Focus on feeling temperature differences.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand why they feel warmer playing in sunny areas and why cars get hot in parking lots
lessons.visualSupports: Temperature comparison charts, sun heating diagram, thermometer reading guides with simple pictures

lessons.title: D'autres sources de chaleur
lessons.oneGoal: Students will identify different sources of heat in their environment and understand that heat can come from many sources

decisionPoints.question: Which heat sources are safe for students to observe and discuss?
decisionPoints.guidance: If classroom heating available: Observe heaters/radiators safely. If limited heat sources: Use pictures and safe demonstrations.

decisionPoints.question: Should we categorize heat sources or focus on identifying them?
decisionPoints.guidance: If categorizing skills strong: Sort into natural vs artificial heat. If identification focus: Simply name and locate heat sources.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for comparing natural vs artificial heat sources?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comparison skills developing: Create clear categories with examples. If advanced: Discuss advantages of different heat sources.

lessons.opening: Heat source mystery (5 min): Show pictures of various heat sources (fireplace, heater, stove, body heat). Students guess what makes each one warm.
lessons.mainActivity: Heat source exploration (25 min): Identify heat sources in classroom and school: heaters, computers, lights, human bodies, friction (rubbing hands). Sort heat sources into categories: sun, electrical, human body, fire, friction. Students create heat source maps of classroom and home. Practice vocabulary: 'Cette source de chaleur est...', 'Nous utilisons cette chaleur pour...'. Safely feel warmth from appropriate sources like heater vents or warm computers.
lessons.closing: Heat source appreciation circle (10 min): Students share their favorite heat source and explain how it helps them. Discuss how different heat sources are used for different purposes.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If safety concerns: Use only pictures and discussion for dangerous heat sources. If too many categories: Focus on sun vs other sources. If concepts overwhelming: Limit to 4-5 familiar heat sources.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students recognize heaters at home, warm clothing from dryers, and heat from cooking, understanding multiple ways to stay warm
lessons.visualSupports: Heat source identification cards, safe vs unsafe heat source charts, heat source category sorting mats

lessons.title: Garder la chaleur en hiver
lessons.oneGoal: Students will understand how insulation works and explore materials that help keep heat in during winter

decisionPoints.question: What insulation materials are safe and effective for classroom demonstrations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If variety of materials available: Compare effectiveness of different insulators. If limited materials: Focus on common insulating materials like fabric and paper.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on clothing insulation or building insulation concepts?
decisionPoints.guidance: If clothing concepts clearer: Start with winter coat examples. If building concepts accessible: Include house insulation discussion.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for insulation effectiveness comparisons?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comparison skills strong: Test different materials systematically. If developing: Focus on insulated vs non-insulated examples.

lessons.opening: Winter clothing investigation (5 min): Students feel different winter clothing items (coat, thin shirt, mittens) and predict which would keep them warmest outside.
lessons.mainActivity: Insulation exploration (25 min): Test various materials as insulators: wrap identical warm objects (like warm water bottles) in different materials (cotton, wool, plastic, paper, foil). Feel and compare how well each material keeps warmth in. Create insulation testing charts. Examine winter clothing and discuss how layers trap warm air. Practice vocabulary: 'Ce matériel garde la chaleur', 'L'isolation nous protège du froid'. Compare thick vs thin materials.
lessons.closing: Insulation fashion show (10 min): Students show how they would dress for winter weather, explaining which materials help keep them warm and why layering works.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If materials get messy: Use sealed containers for testing. If concepts too complex: Focus on thick vs thin material comparisons. If testing unclear: Use obvious temperature differences.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand why winter coats are thick, why houses have insulation, and how blankets keep them warm at night
lessons.visualSupports: Insulation material comparison chart, winter clothing layering diagram, insulation effectiveness ranking sheet

lessons.title: Expérience: tester l'isolation
lessons.oneGoal: Students will conduct experiments to test which materials are best at keeping things warm

decisionPoints.question: What safe materials can effectively demonstrate insulation principles?
decisionPoints.guidance: If ice available safely: Use ice cube insulation tests. If warm water safer: Test keeping warm objects warm instead.

decisionPoints.question: Should we use ice cubes or warm water for insulation testing?
decisionPoints.guidance: If ice manageable: Use ice melting comparisons. If warm water available: Test temperature retention over time.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for measuring and comparing insulation effectiveness?
decisionPoints.guidance: If measurement skills emerging: Use simple comparisons and timing. If advanced: Include temperature readings and data recording.

lessons.opening: Insulation prediction ceremony (5 min): Show identical ice cubes and different wrapping materials. Students predict which wrapping will keep ice frozen longest and explain their thinking.
lessons.mainActivity: Insulation effectiveness experiment (25 min): Wrap identical ice cubes in different materials: bare (control), thin paper, thick fabric, cotton balls, aluminum foil. Place in identical containers and observe which ice melts slowest. Record observations every 5 minutes with drawings and simple words. Alternative: Use warm water in containers with different insulation and measure temperature retention. Create experiment recording sheets comparing predictions vs results.
lessons.closing: Scientific conclusion sharing (10 min): Students share experiment results and explain which materials work best as insulators. Connect to real world: best insulators are like best winter clothing materials.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If ice melts too quickly: Use larger cubes or cooler room. If timing difficult: Focus on final results rather than timed observations. If materials get wet: Use waterproof containers.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand scientific reasons why certain winter clothing materials work better and how insulation keeps homes warm
lessons.visualSupports: Experiment setup diagram, prediction vs results charts, insulation effectiveness ranking poster

lessons.title: Lumière et chaleur des animaux
lessons.oneGoal: Students will explore how some animals create their own light or use heat to survive in winter

decisionPoints.question: Which animal light/heat examples are most accessible to Grade 1 students?
decisionPoints.guidance: If bioluminescence interests students: Use firefly examples and videos. If heat focus preferred: Discuss warm-blooded animals and winter survival.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on bioluminescence or animal heat adaptations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If light creation fascinating: Explore fireflies and deep-sea creatures. If heat survival more relevant: Focus on animal warming strategies.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for comparing animal and human heat strategies?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comparison skills strong: Create detailed comparison charts. If developing: Focus on similarities like needing warmth.

lessons.opening: Animal light mystery (5 min): Show pictures of firefly, glowing fish, and regular animals. Ask students which animals can make their own light and how they might do it.
lessons.mainActivity: Animal energy exploration (25 min): Explore animals that create light (fireflies, some fish, jellyfish) using videos and pictures. Investigate how animals create heat: body warmth, movement, huddling together. Compare cold-blooded vs warm-blooded animals in winter. Students create animal energy journals showing different animals' light and heat strategies. Practice vocabulary: 'Cet animal crée sa propre lumière', 'Les animaux à sang chaud gardent leur chaleur'.
lessons.closing: Animal adaptation celebration (10 min): Students choose an animal and demonstrate how it creates light or stays warm. Discuss amazing ways animals meet their energy needs.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If bioluminescence too complex: Focus on simple examples like fireflies. If heat concepts difficult: Use obvious examples like birds fluffing feathers. If videos unavailable: Use clear photographs and storytelling.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students observe fireflies in summer, understand why cats seek warm spots, and learn how birds survive cold winters
lessons.visualSupports: Bioluminescent animal pictures, animal heat strategy charts, warm-blooded vs cold-blooded comparison diagrams

lessons.title: Faire des reflets avec la lumière
lessons.oneGoal: Students will discover how mirrors and shiny surfaces reflect light and can redirect light beams

decisionPoints.question: What reflective surfaces are safe and produce clear reflections for students?
decisionPoints.guidance: If mirrors available: Use unbreakable mirrors for safety. If limited mirrors: Use water, foil, and other shiny surfaces.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on mirror reflections or various reflective materials?
decisionPoints.guidance: If mirror skills developing: Focus on mirror use and reflection basics. If exploration preferred: Try many different reflective surfaces.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for directing reflected light beams?
decisionPoints.guidance: If light direction concepts emerging: Try simple light redirection activities. If advanced: Create light pathway challenges.

lessons.opening: Reflection magic show (5 min): Use mirror to reflect flashlight beam onto wall. Ask students how light 'bounced' from flashlight to mirror to wall.
lessons.mainActivity: Reflection laboratory (25 min): Students experiment with various reflective surfaces: mirrors, water in bowls, aluminum foil, shiny metal. Use flashlights to create reflections and try to direct reflected light to different targets. Explore what makes good reflectors vs poor reflectors. Create reflection art by bouncing light patterns onto walls. Practice vocabulary: 'La lumière rebondit', 'Le miroir fait un reflet', 'Je peux diriger la lumière'.
lessons.closing: Reflection light show (10 min): Students create group light show using mirrors and flashlights to make patterns on walls. Discuss how reflections help us see around corners and make rooms brighter.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If mirrors create chaos: Use structured rotation system. If reflections unclear: Ensure strong light sources and good contrast. If safety concerns: Use plastic mirrors and supervise closely.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand how bathroom mirrors work, why water looks shiny, and how reflective surfaces can make dark areas brighter
lessons.visualSupports: Light reflection diagram showing angle concepts, reflective vs non-reflective material examples, light path illustrations

lessons.title: Couleurs dans la lumière
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe how white light contains many colors and explore simple light spectrum concepts

decisionPoints.question: What safe methods can demonstrate light spectrum to young learners?
decisionPoints.guidance: If prisms available: Use prisms for clear spectrum demonstration. If soap bubbles safer: Focus on bubble rainbow colors.

decisionPoints.question: Should we use prisms, water, or soap bubbles for color demonstrations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If prisms work well: Use for controlled spectrum creation. If water/soap bubbles more engaging: Focus on natural rainbow creation.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for understanding white light composition?
decisionPoints.guidance: If color mixing concepts emerging: Explore how colors combine. If too complex: Focus on finding colors hidden in white light.

lessons.opening: Rainbow hunt (5 min): Ask students when they've seen rainbows and what colors they remember. Show how white light can be 'broken' into colors.
lessons.mainActivity: Color discovery laboratory (25 min): Use prisms, water sprays, or soap bubbles to create rainbow colors from white light. Students observe and name colors they see: rouge, orange, jaune, vert, bleu, violet. Try making rainbows in different ways and locations around classroom. Create color spectrum journals documenting their discoveries. Compare artificial rainbows to natural rainbows in photos. Practice vocabulary: 'La lumière blanche contient toutes les couleurs', 'Je vois un arc-en-ciel'.
lessons.closing: Rainbow celebration dance (10 min): Students create movements for each color of the rainbow and sing about colors hidden in light. Discuss where else they might look for light colors.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If prisms don't work: Use soap bubbles or water spray near windows. If colors unclear: Ensure bright light source and good positioning. If concepts too advanced: Focus on color identification rather than light composition.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students connect to rainbows they see after rain, colors in soap bubbles, and understanding why sunlight creates beautiful colors
lessons.visualSupports: Rainbow color sequence charts, light spectrum diagrams, natural rainbow photographs

lessons.title: Notre journal de lumière et chaleur
lessons.oneGoal: Students will document their discoveries about light and heat sources through scientific recording and observation logs

decisionPoints.question: What documentation format works best for Grade 1 scientific recording?
decisionPoints.guidance: If writing skills emerging: Use mostly drawings with simple labels. If writing developing: Include more detailed descriptions and measurements.

decisionPoints.question: Should we include drawings, measurements, or written observations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comprehensive documentation wanted: Include all types of recording. If time limited: Focus on drawings and simple vocabulary.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for organizing their learning into categories?
decisionPoints.guidance: If organization skills developing: Provide clear categories with examples. If advanced: Let students create their own organizational system.

lessons.opening: Scientific author introduction (5 min): Review all the light and heat discoveries made throughout the unit. Explain that scientists document their findings so others can learn from their work.
lessons.mainActivity: Science journal creation (25 min): Students compile their learning into comprehensive light and heat journals. Include pages for: light sources, shadow experiments, heat sources, insulation testing, animal adaptations, reflection discoveries, color observations. Add drawings, simple writing, photos from experiments, and key vocabulary. Students organize their favorite discoveries and most important learning. Create journal covers showing light and heat themes.
lessons.closing: Journal sharing celebration (10 min): Students present their favorite page from their science journal and explain one important thing they learned about light and heat. Plan to share journals with families.
materials: All previous lesson materials and documentation
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If journal creation overwhelming: Focus on 3-4 key discoveries only. If writing challenging: Use teacher scribing and student illustration. If organization difficult: Provide pre-made journal templates.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students learn how scientists keep careful records and understand the importance of documenting discoveries to share knowledge
lessons.visualSupports: Journal page templates, vocabulary reference charts from all lessons, scientific documentation examples

lessons.title: Économiser l'énergie lumineuse
lessons.oneGoal: Students will understand energy conservation and learn simple ways to save light energy in winter (extension)

decisionPoints.question: Which energy conservation concepts are appropriate for Grade 1 understanding?
decisionPoints.guidance: If conservation concepts emerging: Focus on turning off unused lights. If environmental awareness developing: Include broader energy-saving ideas.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on turning off lights or using natural light more?
decisionPoints.guidance: If light switching accessible: Emphasize on/off conservation. If natural light concepts clear: Focus on daylight utilization.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for discussing environmental responsibility?
decisionPoints.guidance: If responsibility concepts developing: Include simple environmental care ideas. If too complex: Focus on practical energy saving only.

lessons.opening: Energy detective introduction (5 min): Students become 'energy detectives' looking for ways to save light energy at school and home.
lessons.mainActivity: Energy conservation exploration (25 min): Identify opportunities to save light energy: turning off lights in empty rooms, using daylight instead of artificial lights when possible, choosing efficient light sources. Create energy-saving action plans for classroom and home. Practice vocabulary: 'Nous économisons l'énergie', 'Éteignons les lumières inutiles'. Design energy-saving reminder signs for classroom.
lessons.closing: Energy-saving commitment ceremony (10 min): Students make personal commitments to save light energy and share ideas with families. Create classroom energy-saving goals.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If concepts too complex: Focus only on light switching. If overwhelming: Choose 2-3 simple conservation actions. If responsibility heavy: Keep tone positive and empowering.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students develop habits of turning off lights, using daylight, and understanding their role in energy conservation
lessons.visualSupports: Energy-saving action charts, light usage tracking sheets, conservation reminder posters

lessons.title: Lumière et chaleur dans d'autres pays
lessons.oneGoal: Students will explore how people in different climates use light and heat differently (extension)

decisionPoints.question: Which global examples best illustrate different light/heat needs?
decisionPoints.guidance: If geography concepts emerging: Use obvious climate contrasts like Arctic vs tropical. If world awareness developing: Include varied cultural examples.

decisionPoints.question: Should we compare arctic vs tropical heat needs or seasonal differences?
decisionPoints.guidance: If extreme contrasts clearer: Focus on very hot vs very cold places. If seasonal patterns interesting: Compare different seasonal experiences.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for simple geography and climate connections?
decisionPoints.guidance: If geography skills developing: Use globe and simple climate concepts. If too complex: Focus on pictures and obvious differences.

lessons.opening: Global climate tour (5 min): Use globe to show different climate zones. Ask students to predict how people in very cold vs very hot places might use light and heat differently.
lessons.mainActivity: World light and heat exploration (25 min): Compare how people in different climates meet light and heat needs: Arctic igloos vs tropical open-air homes, seasonal festivals with lights in different cultures, how people dress for different climates. Create world climate comparison charts. Students choose a climate different from theirs and design solutions for light and heat needs.
lessons.closing: Global appreciation circle (10 min): Students share their favorite global light or heat solution and discuss how people everywhere need light and heat but solve challenges differently.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If geography too complex: Use simple hot/cold place comparisons. If cultural content overwhelming: Focus on physical climate needs only. If concepts abstract: Use lots of visual examples.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students appreciate global diversity in meeting basic light and heat needs and understand universal human requirements
lessons.visualSupports: World climate map with pictures, cultural light/heat solution examples, climate comparison charts

lessons.title: Inventer des solutions de chaleur
lessons.oneGoal: Students will design simple inventions to solve winter heating problems using their knowledge of heat sources (extension)

decisionPoints.question: What design challenges are appropriate for Grade 1 problem-solving skills?
decisionPoints.guidance: If design thinking emerging: Provide structured invention challenges. If creativity strong: Allow open-ended invention opportunities.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on personal warming devices or room heating solutions?
decisionPoints.guidance: If personal solutions more accessible: Design hand warmers or heated clothing. If room heating interesting: Create model heating systems.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for invention planning and simple engineering design?
decisionPoints.guidance: If planning skills developing: Use step-by-step design process. If advanced: Include testing and improvement cycles.

lessons.opening: Inventor introduction (5 min): Students become inventors solving winter heating problems. Review heat sources and insulation knowledge to prepare for design challenges.
lessons.mainActivity: Heat invention workshop (25 min): Students design inventions to solve heating problems: keeping hands warm outdoors, heating a cold room, staying warm while camping. Use drawings and available materials to create invention prototypes. Apply knowledge of heat sources, insulation, and heat transfer. Present inventions explaining how they work using scientific vocabulary.
lessons.closing: Invention showcase (10 min): Students present their heating inventions and explain how they used their scientific knowledge to solve problems. Celebrate creative problem-solving.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If invention too complex: Provide simpler design challenges. If materials unavailable: Focus on drawing and explaining designs. If presentation overwhelming: Use show-and-tell format.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand how inventors create new heating solutions and how scientific knowledge leads to practical inventions
lessons.visualSupports: Design process steps, invention planning templates, heat source reference charts

lessons.title: Lumière et chaleur pour les plantes d'hiver
lessons.oneGoal: Students will investigate how plants need light and heat to survive winter indoors (extension)

decisionPoints.question: Which plants best demonstrate winter light and heat needs?
decisionPoints.guidance: If classroom plants available: Use existing plants for observation. If no plants: Use simple growing experiments with seeds.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on houseplants or greenhouse concepts?
decisionPoints.guidance: If houseplant care accessible: Focus on indoor plant needs. If greenhouse concepts interesting: Explore protected growing environments.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for plant care experiments?
decisionPoints.guidance: If plant care skills emerging: Try simple light/heat experiments with plants. If advanced: Include plant care responsibilities and observations.

lessons.opening: Plant winter survival question (5 min): Ask students how outdoor plants survive winter and why houseplants need special care indoors.
lessons.mainActivity: Plant energy needs investigation (25 min): Observe how houseplants are positioned near windows for light and kept warm indoors. Experiment with placing plants in different light and heat conditions to observe growth differences. Create plant care journals documenting light and heat requirements. Connect to plant biology: plants need light for food-making and heat for growth.
lessons.closing: Plant care commitment (10 min): Students make commitments to help care for classroom plants, understanding their light and heat needs. Discuss how understanding plant needs helps us grow food in winter.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If plants unavailable: Use pictures and videos of plant care. If experiments too complex: Focus on observation rather than manipulation. If care overwhelming: Assign simple plant care tasks.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand houseplant care, greenhouse farming, and how understanding plant needs helps provide food year-round
lessons.visualSupports: Plant needs charts, indoor vs outdoor plant comparison pictures, plant care instruction cards

lessons.title: Spectacle de lumière scientifique
lessons.oneGoal: Students will create a light demonstration show sharing their discoveries about light sources, shadows, and reflections (extension)

decisionPoints.question: What light demonstrations are safe for students to perform?
decisionPoints.guidance: If performance skills strong: Include multiple demonstration types. If safety primary: Focus on simple, safe light activities.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on shadow play or light source demonstrations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If shadow skills developed: Create shadow puppet shows. If light science focus: Demonstrate different light properties.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for teaching others about their discoveries?
decisionPoints.guidance: If teaching skills emerging: Use show-and-tell format. If advanced: Include explanation and audience interaction.

lessons.opening: Science showtime preparation (5 min): Students prepare to become science demonstrators, sharing their light and heat knowledge through performances.
lessons.mainActivity: Light science show creation (25 min): Students create demonstrations showcasing their learning: shadow puppet shows, light reflection displays, color spectrum demonstrations, heat source explanations. Practice using scientific vocabulary while entertaining audiences. Prepare materials and practice presentations.
lessons.closing: Dress rehearsal performance (10 min): Students perform their light demonstrations for classmates, practicing their scientist presentation skills. Prepare for family science show.
materials: All demonstration materials from previous lessons
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If performances too complex: Simplify to basic demonstrations. If stage fright issues: Use partner presentations. If materials unavailable: Focus on explanation and discussion.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students learn how scientists share knowledge through demonstrations and develop confidence in scientific communication
lessons.visualSupports: Demonstration setup guides, scientific vocabulary cue cards, performance planning templates

lessons.title: Célébration: petits experts en lumière et chaleur
lessons.oneGoal: Students will celebrate their learning journey by sharing light and heat knowledge with families through interactive demonstrations (extension)

decisionPoints.question: How can the celebration showcase each student's understanding of light and heat concepts?
decisionPoints.guidance: If individual recognition important: Provide individual presentation opportunities. If group celebration preferred: Create collaborative demonstration stations.

decisionPoints.question: Should we include hands-on experiments or demonstration stations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If interactive engagement desired: Set up hands-on activity stations. If showcase format preferred: Focus on student presentations and displays.

decisionPoints.question: What activities best show student growth to families?
decisionPoints.guidance: If learning journey important: Include before/after documentation. If knowledge demonstration focus: Emphasize current understanding and skills.

lessons.opening: Expert scientist preparation (5 min): Students put on their scientist roles and prepare to share their expertise about light and heat with families.
lessons.mainActivity: Family light and heat celebration (25 min): Students guide families through interactive stations: shadow experiments, insulation testing, light reflection activities, heat source identification, color spectrum creation. Students explain their discoveries using scientific vocabulary and demonstrate their understanding. Families participate in experiments and ask questions about student learning.
lessons.closing: Scientific achievement ceremony (10 min): Celebrate student growth as light and heat scientists. Present certificates recognizing specific achievements and discoveries. Students share their favorite learning from the unit.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If family participation varies: Provide alternative celebration activities for students without family present. If overwhelming: Focus on 2-3 key demonstration stations. If timing challenging: Allow flexible station participation.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students proudly share their scientific learning with families, building community appreciation for science education and light/heat understanding
lessons.visualSupports: Learning journey display, scientific vocabulary posters, experiment result documentation, achievement recognition materials
